pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Rocks and soil

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Science, Year 3 Rocks):** Pupils recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-ESS supports; soils as weathered Earth materials):** Recognise soil as broken-down rock plus decayed living matter, and that different soils have different properties.

- **Operational details:** The load-bearing idea is that soil is a MIXTURE — tiny broken-down rock particles plus decomposed organic matter (humus) — not a single 'brown stuff'. Children compare soil types (sandy, clay, loam) by observable and testable properties: particle size, how gritty or sticky it feels, and especially how fast water drains through (a percolation test). A second big idea is TIME: rock breaks down into soil incredibly slowly, over very long periods. Build understanding through hands-on investigation — examine soils with a lens, do a settling jar (particles sort into layers) and a drainage comparison — then link back to prior rock-property work: soil starts as rock.
bestPractices: Teach soil as a MIXTURE of broken rock + organic matter; separate the two components explicitly (a settling jar shows sand/silt/clay layers with humus floating on top).
Compare soil types (sandy vs clay vs loam) by testable properties, especially a fair drainage/percolation test with equal water and time.
Use hands-on investigation with hand lenses and jars — soil properties are felt and observed, not told.
Connect to prior rock work: soil begins as rock that has been broken down, and this takes a very long time.
Draw out why soil type matters (drainage affects which plants grow) to make the properties meaningful.
keyRepresentations: A settling jar showing soil separating into layers (stones, sand, silt, clay, floating humus).
A drainage/percolation comparison of sandy vs clay vs loam soils.
A soil-profile / cutaway diagram (organic layer over broken rock over bedrock).
A soil-property comparison table (gritty/sticky, drains fast/slow, colour).
commonMisconceptions: 'Soil is just dirt / one single substance' — not seeing it as a mixture of rock particles and organic matter.
'Soil has nothing to do with rock' — missing that soil is broken-down rock.
'All soils are the same' — not distinguishing sandy, clay and loam by property.
'Soil forms quickly' — underestimating the very long time rock takes to break down.
'Clay soil is best because it holds water' or 'sandy is best because it drains' — treating one soil as universally superior rather than suited to different conditions.

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds: soil is a MIXTURE of broken-down rock particles (sand, silt, clay) plus decomposed organic matter (humus), not a single 'brown stuff'. Children investigate by hand — a settling jar separates soil into layers, a fair drainage test compares soil types, and a hand lens reveals rock grains and leaf bits. A second big idea is TIME: rock breaks down into soil very slowly. Hands-on investigation with real local soil is the core experience; cutaway diagrams, profiles and sorting tasks support vocabulary and classification.

activities.title: Settling jar: watch soil pull apart into its parts
feedback: If a learner says 'it's all just dirt', point to the separated layers: 'The stones and sand that sank are broken-down rock; the dark floating bits are rotted plants — that's two different things mixed together.'
If a learner denies any link to rock, direct attention to the gritty sand and stones at the bottom: 'Those grains are tiny pieces of rock.'
Praise naming each layer and saying where it came from, not just listing colours.
activities.rationale: Separating the components physically makes the abstract 'mixture' idea observable, addressing the misconception that soil is a single substance and the misconception that soil has nothing to do with rock.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter.
Soil is a mixture of weathered rock particles (sand/silt/clay) and decomposed organic matter (humus); soil types differ in particle size and drainage; soil formation is very slow.
learnerActions: Scoop soil into a clear jar and fill with water, leaving space at the top.
Put the lid on, shake well, then set the jar down and leave it to settle.

Watch and record what settles first, what settles last, and what floats — you will typically see heavy stones and sand sink first, finer silt next, cloudy clay settle slowly on top, and dark bits of rotted leaf (humus) float; write down what you actually observe, as real soils vary.
Draw and label the layers you see, naming which are broken-down rock and which are once-living matter.
Use a hand lens on a pinch of dry soil to spot rock grains and small pieces of plant material up close.
activities.intendedInsight: Soil is a mixture: it separates into broken-down rock particles (sand/silt/clay) plus decomposed plant matter (humus), so it is not one single substance.

activities.title: Fair drainage race: sandy vs clay vs loam
feedback: If a learner says 'all soils are the same', contrast the drainage times they actually measured, for example: 'Look how much faster the water came through the sandy one than the clay one.' (Use the class's real results; dry, cracked clay can sometimes let water through quickly at first.)
If a learner claims one soil is simply best, ask 'best for what?' — clay holds water, sand drains quickly; each suits different conditions.
Reinforce the fair-test idea: 'We used the same amount of soil, the same amount of water, the same-sized funnels and the same timing, so the difference is most likely caused by the type of soil.'
activities.rationale: A controlled comparison lets children distinguish soil types by measurable properties and challenges both the 'all soils are the same' and 'one soil is universally best' misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Soil is a mixture of weathered rock particles (sand/silt/clay) and decomposed organic matter (humus); soil types differ in particle size and drainage; soil formation is very slow.
learnerActions: Set up three funnels or pots, one with sandy soil, one with clay soil, one with loam, each with the same amount of soil.
Pour the SAME amount of water into each at the same time to make it a fair test.
Watch and time how fast water drains through each, and record which is fastest and slowest.
Feel each soil (with permission) and note whether it is gritty or sticky.
Describe how the soils differ and suggest why a plant might prefer one soil over another.
activities.intendedInsight: Different soils have different, testable properties: water drains fast through sandy soil and slowly through clay, and these differences matter for which plants grow well — no single soil is universally 'best'.

activities.title: Soil profile and the slow story of soil
feedback: If a learner thinks soil 'was always there', connect to the profile: 'The solid rock at the bottom slowly crumbles into the loose soil above — it took a very long time.'
If a learner thinks soil forms quickly, emphasise the long timescale: rock breaks down over very many years, not overnight.
Reward answers that name both the rock origin and the once-living (humus) origin.
activities.rationale: A labelled profile gives vocabulary and a spatial story that supports the time/formation idea; it is a scaffold for the hands-on tests, not a replacement for them.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter.
Soil is a mixture of weathered rock particles (sand/silt/clay) and decomposed organic matter (humus); soil types differ in particle size and drainage; soil formation is very slow.
learnerActions: Examine a soil-profile cutaway (organic layer on top, broken rock below, solid bedrock at the bottom) and label each layer.
For each layer, say what it is and where it came from.
Discuss or write how the solid rock below slowly breaks apart over a very long time to make the loose particles above it.
Use a lift-the-flap or 'what is soil made of?' task to recall the two main ingredients: broken rock and humus.
activities.intendedInsight: Soil forms slowly as rock gradually breaks apart over very long periods into particles that mix with decomposed living matter; in a profile like this one, the layers show that journey from solid bedrock up to soil (some soils instead form from rock pieces carried in by rivers, ice or wind).

activities.title: Sort and match soils by property
feedback: If a learner picks only 'rock' or only 'dead plants' as what soil is made of, remind them it is BOTH mixed together.
If a learner mismatches drainage, link back to the drainage race results.
Note: sorting and matching check recall and classification; they do not by themselves show a learner can run or reason through an investigation — pair them with the hands-on benches.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and matching give clean practice and checking of vocabulary and classification, complementing the investigative work. Recognition tasks can confirm classification but do not on their own elicit a learner independently constructing an explanation.
sourceClaims: Soil is a mixture of weathered rock particles (sand/silt/clay) and decomposed organic matter (humus); soil types differ in particle size and drainage; soil formation is very slow.
learnerActions: Sort soil cards or samples into gritty vs sticky groups.
Match each soil type (sandy, clay, loam) to its drainage speed (fast, slow, in between).
Answer: 'What is soil made of?' choosing the answer that names both broken-down rock and decomposed organic matter.
For plants: discuss why a soil's drainage might help or hinder certain plants.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can classify soils by observable properties and articulate that soil's two core ingredients are broken rock and humus.

constraints: Use real jars of local soil and a real percolation test as the essential hands-on complement; on-screen settling jars and drainage races are simulations that preview or review, consistent with the KS2 practical-science expectation for felt, observed investigation.
Keep the drainage comparison a fair test: equal soil amounts, equal water, equal time — otherwise differences cannot be attributed to the soil type.

A soil-profile diagram or on-screen cutaway supports vocabulary and the formation story but cannot deliver the drainage comparison that distinguishes soil types; use it alongside, not instead of, the tests.
Sorting/matching/multiple-choice tasks check recall and classification; they do not require learners to construct or run an investigation.
Avoid teaching any one soil as universally 'best' — frame clay (holds water) and sand (drains fast) as suited to different conditions.
Correct the 'plants eat soil' idea where it arises: plants take water and minerals from soil and make their own food by photosynthesis; soil is not consumed as food.
A dig-down 3D soil pit can give a spatial sense of horizons but is optional; the learning target is composition, drainage and formation time, which a labelled cutaway can also convey.
reviewNotes: Independent re-review: both prior corrections were verified present — activities[2].intendedInsight no longer states 'top down' and is consistent with its feedback (bedrock below crumbles upward), and activities[0] records observation rather than prescribing the outcome. No new critical learner-facing errors found.

This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both cited sources are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims about soil composition, drainage differences by particle size, and slow formation come from DfE KS2 and USDA NRCS; these support the general principles but do not establish efficacy of any specific activity above.

Settling-jar layer order (stones/sand sink, silt, then clay; humus floats) reflects the row's description. Real-world results vary with soil composition and how long it is left; treat observed layers as approximate rather than guaranteed, and let children record what they actually see.

The original row asserts '3D adds little' and that dialogue 'can't run the tests'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; softened to scoped notes about affordances rather than universal claims.
Hand-lens/jar interactivity examples (zoom to reveal grains, shake-and-settle, timed funnels) are retained as concrete learning mechanisms, not mandated implementations.

probeDeeper: If you rubbed two rocks together for a very long time, how could that help make soil?
Are all soils the same? How do sandy soil and clay soil behave differently with water?
Do plants eat the soil? What do they actually get from it?
assess.correctAnswer: Soil is made over a very long time as rock gradually breaks down into tiny particles, mixed with decomposed plant and animal matter (humus). So soil comes partly from broken-down rock and partly from once-living things — it didn't just appear.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Soil has always just been there and isn't made of anything'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Soil forms as rock weathers and organisms decompose, over a very long time.
errorPatterns.distractor: Soil has always been there; it isn't made from anything.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Soil has nothing to do with rock'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Look at the sand and grit in soil — those are broken-down rock particles.
errorPatterns.distractor: Soil has nothing to do with rock.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Plants eat the soil / soil is the plant's food'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Soil gives water, minerals and support; plants make their own food by photosynthesis.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats soil as food that is consumed

errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare sandy, clay and loam soils — how they feel and drain water.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks soil was always there or has no link to rock.
responseLevels.full: Explains that soil forms slowly from broken-down rock mixed with decomposed organic matter, compares soil types by their properties, and knows plants take water and minerals from soil rather than eating it.
responseLevels.partial: Says soil comes from rock OR contains dead plants but not both, or thinks all soils are alike.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Where does soil come from — has it always just been there, or is it made from something? And what is soil actually made of?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks soil is just dirt that was always there, or who sees no link to rock, differs from one who knows soil forms from broken-down rock plus organic matter over a long time.
